rows.subtopic: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier
rows.stem: An ac voltage \(V = 0.5 \sin(100\pi t)\) volt is applied, in turn, across a half-wave rectifier and a full-wave rectifier. The frequency of the output voltage across them respectively will be
rows.context: A pure semiconductor like Ge or Si, when doped with a small amount of suitable impurity, becomes an extrinsic semiconductor. In thermal equilibrium, the electron and hole concentration in it are related to the concentration of intrinsic charge carriers. A p-type or n-type semiconductor can be converted into a p-n junction by doping it with suitable impurity. Two processes, diffusion and drift take place during formation of a p-n junction. A semiconductor diode is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for the application of an external voltage. A p-n junction diode allows currents to pass only in one direction when it is forward biased. Due to this property, a diode is widely used to rectify alternating voltages, in half-wave or full wave configuration.
rows.solution:
First the input frequency:

\(V = 0{\cdot}5\sin(100\pi t) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \omega = 100\pi\ \mathrm{rad/s}\)

\(f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{100\pi}{2\pi} = 50\ \text{Hz}\)

**Half-wave rectifier.** A single diode conducts on one half of each input cycle and blocks the other. One pulse of output appears per input cycle, so the output repeats at the input frequency:

\(f_{\text{half}} = 50\ \text{Hz}\)

**Full-wave rectifier.** Both halves of the input cycle are made to drive current through the load in the same direction, so *two* pulses appear per input cycle and the output repeats twice as often:

\(f_{\text{full}} = 100\ \text{Hz}\)

So 50 Hz and 100 Hz respectively, option (D).

The doubling is why full-wave rectification is preferred in practice: the output not only carries twice the average power but has its ripple at twice the frequency, which a given smoothing capacitor filters far more effectively. The amplitude \(0{\cdot}5\) V is not used at all — the question asks only about frequency.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm and a thin diverging lens of focal length 15 cm are placed coaxially in contact. The power of the combination is
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification.
rows.solution:
For thin lenses in contact the powers add. With focal lengths in metres:

Converging lens: \(f_1 = +20\ \text{cm} = +0{\cdot}20\ \text{m}\), so \(P_1 = \dfrac{1}{0{\cdot}20} = +5\ \mathrm{D}\)

Diverging lens: \(f_2 = -15\ \text{cm} = -0{\cdot}15\ \text{m}\), so \(P_2 = \dfrac{1}{-0{\cdot}15} = -\dfrac{20}{3}\ \mathrm{D}\)

\(P = P_1 + P_2 = 5 - \dfrac{20}{3} = \dfrac{15 - 20}{3} = -\dfrac{5}{3}\ \mathrm{D}\)

The answer is (B).

Two details decide it. The diverging lens must carry a **negative** focal length, and the focal lengths must be in **metres** before inverting — leaving them in centimetres would give a power a hundred times too large. The result being negative means the shorter-focus diverging lens wins: the combination behaves as a diverging lens of focal length \(-0{\cdot}6\) m.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: The radii of curvature of two surfaces of a convex lens are R and 2R. If the focal length of this lens is \(\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)\mathrm{R}\), the refractive index of the material of the lens is :
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification.
rows.solution:
Apply the lens-maker's formula to a convex lens whose two surfaces have radii \(R\) and \(2R\). For a biconvex lens the first surface is convex towards the incoming light and the second concave towards it, so in the Cartesian convention \(R_1 = +R\) and \(R_2 = -2R\):

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) = (n - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R} + \dfrac{1}{2R}\right) = (n - 1)\dfrac{3}{2R}\)

Given \(f = \dfrac{4R}{3}\):

\(\dfrac{3}{4R} = (n - 1)\dfrac{3}{2R}\)

\(n - 1 = \dfrac{3}{4R} \times \dfrac{2R}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(n = \dfrac{3}{2}\)

The answer is (C).

The sign convention on \(R_2\) is what the question is testing. Taking both radii as positive would give \(\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\frac{1}{2R}\) and hence \(n = 1 + \frac{3}{2} = 2{\cdot}5\), which is not offered — and would be an implausibly high index for lens glass. The answer \(1{\cdot}5\) is exactly the value of ordinary crown glass, a useful check that the convention was applied correctly.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: The focal length of an equiconvex lens
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification.

options.label: A
options.text: increases when the lens is dipped in water.

options.label: B
options.text: increases when the wavelength of incident light decreases.

options.label: C
options.text: increases with decrease in radius of curvature of its surface.

options.label: D
options.text: decreases when the lens is cut into two identical parts along its principal axis.

rows.solution:
The lens-maker's formula written for a lens in a medium makes the dependence explicit:

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_{\text{lens}}}{n_{\text{medium}}} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\)

Dipping the lens in water raises \(n_{\text{medium}}\) from 1 to about \(1{\cdot}33\), so the bracket \(\left(\frac{n_{\text{lens}}}{n_{\text{medium}}} - 1\right)\) shrinks. With everything else unchanged, \(1/f\) falls and **\(f\) increases**.

The answer is (A).

For glass of \(n = 1{\cdot}5\) the bracket drops from \(0{\cdot}5\) to \(\frac{1{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}33} - 1 \approx 0{\cdot}13\), so the focal length grows nearly fourfold — the lens becomes much weaker, because refraction depends on the *contrast* in refractive index and water has reduced it.

The others fail on inspection. **(B)**: shorter wavelength means higher \(n\), hence shorter \(f\) — this is dispersion, and it is why violet focuses nearer than red. **(C)**: \(f\) is proportional to \(R\), so a smaller radius of curvature means a *shorter* focal length. **(D)**: cutting a lens along its principal axis halves the aperture but leaves both surface curvatures untouched, so \(f\) does not change at all — only the brightness of the image does.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A thin convex lens L of focal length 10 cm and a concave mirror M of focal length 15 cm are placed coaxially 40 cm apart as shown in figure. A beam of light coming parallel to the principal axis is incident on the lens. The final image will be formed at a distance of
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — every option is expressed as 'left of lens' or 'right of lens', and which way is left is fixed only by the drawn direction of the incoming beam. Described here without stating the result: a horizontal dashed principal axis; a biconvex lens labelled L drawn on the left with four horizontal ray arrows approaching it; a concave mirror labelled M drawn on the right with its reflecting side facing the lens; and the lens-to-mirror separation marked 40 cm by a double-headed arrow. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
Follow the light one element at a time.

**Through the lens.** The incident beam is parallel to the principal axis, so the lens brings it to a focus at its own focal point, 10 cm to its right.

**On to the mirror.** That focus is not where the mirror is — the mirror stands 40 cm from the lens — so the light converges at 10 cm, crosses over, and diverges onwards, reaching the mirror as if from a real object \(40 - 10 = 30\) cm in front of it.

**At the mirror.** For the concave mirror, \(u = -30\) cm and \(f = -15\) cm:

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{-15} - \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{-2 + 1}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{30}\)

\(v = -30\ \text{cm}\)

The image forms 30 cm in front of the mirror, on the same side as the object — which places it \(40 - 30 = 10\) cm from the lens, on the lens's right.

**10 cm to the right of the lens**, which is option (B).

The object sat at \(2f\) of the mirror, so its image returns to \(2f\) as well — real, inverted and the same size. That is the one object distance for a concave mirror at which object and image coincide in position.

One further remark, since the light does not simply stop there: those converging rays pass through the image point and then travel on to the lens, arriving 10 cm away — exactly the lens's focal length. Light diverging from a focal point emerges parallel, so the beam finally leaves the system collimated, with no further image at any finite distance. The keyed 10 cm is the image formed by the mirror, which is the last one anywhere in the system.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A beam of light coming parallel to the principal axis of a convex lens \(L_1\) of focal length 16 cm is incident on it. Another convex lens \(L_2\) of focal length 12 cm is placed coaxially at a distance 40 cm from \(L_1\). The nature and distance of the final image from \(L_2\) will be
rows.context: A lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical. Applying the formula of image formation by a single spherical surface successively at the two surfaces of a thin lens, a formula known as lens maker's formula and hence the basic lens formula can be obtained. The focal length (or power) of a lens depends on the radii of its surfaces and the refractive index of its material with respect to the surrounding medium. The refractive index of a material depends on the wavelength of light used. Combination of lenses helps us to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired power and magnification.
rows.solution:
Two lenses in succession, with the first one's image acting as the second one's object.

**At \(L_1\).** The incoming beam is parallel to the axis, so \(L_1\) focuses it at its focal point, \(16\) cm to its right.

**At \(L_2\).** The lenses are 40 cm apart, so that point lies

\(40 - 16 = 24\ \text{cm}\)

to the left of \(L_2\) — a real object for it. With \(u = -24\) cm and \(f = +12\) cm:

\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{-24} = \dfrac{2 - 1}{24} = \dfrac{1}{24}\)

\(v = +24\ \text{cm}\)

A positive \(v\) means the image lies on the far side of \(L_2\), where the light actually goes — so it is **real, 24 cm from \(L_2\)**, option (A).

The object happened to sit at \(2f\) of \(L_2\) (\(24 = 2 \times 12\)), which is why the image comes back at \(2f\) as well, inverted and the same size as the intermediate image. Had the two lenses been 28 cm apart instead, the intermediate image would have landed exactly at the focus of \(L_2\) and the final beam would have emerged parallel — the telescope configuration.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram for the formation of the image of an object by a convex mirror. Hence, obtain the mirror equation.
(ii) Why are multi-component lenses used for both the objective and the eyepiece in optical instruments ?
(iii) The magnification of a small object produced by a compound microscope is 200. The focal length of the eyepiece is 2 cm and the final image is formed at infinity. Find the magnification produced by the objective.
rows.solution:
**(i) Ray diagram and the mirror equation for a convex mirror.**

*The diagram.* Place an object AB upright on the principal axis in front of a convex mirror of pole P, focus F and centre of curvature C, both F and C lying **behind** the mirror. Two rays fix the image:

- a ray from A parallel to the axis, which strikes the mirror at M and is reflected so that it appears to come from F;
- a ray from A directed towards C, which strikes the mirror normally and is reflected straight back along its own path.

The two reflected rays diverge, so they do not meet in front of the mirror; their backward extensions meet behind it at \(A'\). Dropping a perpendicular to the axis gives the image \(A'B'\) — **virtual, erect and diminished**, and lying between P and F whatever the object distance.

*Deriving the equation.* For paraxial rays, MP may be treated as a straight line perpendicular to the axis, so \(PM = AB\).

Right-angled triangles \(A'B'F\) and MPF are similar:

\(\dfrac{B'A'}{PM} = \dfrac{B'F}{FP} \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \dfrac{B'A'}{BA} = \dfrac{B'F}{FP} \qquad \text{...(1)}\)

Since \(\angle APB = \angle A'PB'\) (the laws of reflection at the pole), triangles \(A'PB'\) and APB are also similar:

\(\dfrac{B'A'}{BA} = \dfrac{B'P}{BP} \qquad \text{...(2)}\)

Comparing (1) and (2):

\(\dfrac{B'F}{FP} = \dfrac{B'P}{BP} \qquad\text{and}\qquad B'F = PF - PB'\)

so

\(\dfrac{PF - PB'}{FP} = \dfrac{B'P}{BP}\)

Applying the sign convention — \(PF = f\), \(PB' = +v\), \(PB = -u\) — and simplifying gives

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\)

the mirror equation, which holds for concave and convex mirrors alike once signs are respected.

**(ii) Why multi-component lenses are used.**

A single lens suffers from several **aberrations**: chromatic aberration, because the refractive index varies with wavelength so different colours focus at different points; and monochromatic aberrations such as spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism and distortion. Combining several lenses of different glasses and curvatures lets these defects be made to cancel — an achromatic doublet, for instance, pairs a crown converging lens with a flint diverging one so their chromatic errors oppose. The result is a sharper, brighter, colour-faithful image than any single lens can give.

**(iii) Magnification produced by the objective.**

For a compound microscope the total magnification is the product of the two stages:

\(m = m_o \times m_e\)

With the final image at infinity, the eyepiece works as a simple magnifier in normal adjustment:

\(m_e = \dfrac{D}{f_e} = \dfrac{25}{2} = 12{\cdot}5\)

Hence

\(m_o = \dfrac{m}{m_e} = \dfrac{200}{12{\cdot}5} = 16\)

**The objective produces a magnification of 16.**

rows.stem:
(i) Differentiate between a wavefront and a ray.
(ii) State Huygen's principle and verify laws of reflection using suitable diagram.
(iii) In Young's double slit experiment, the slits \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are 3 mm apart and the screen is placed 1.0 m away from the slits. It is observed that the fourth bright fringe is at a distance of 5 mm from the second dark fringe. Find the wavelength of light used.
rows.solution:
**(i) Wavefront and ray.**

A **wavefront** is a surface on which every point oscillates in the same phase — the locus of points the disturbance has reached at the same instant. A **ray** is the straight line along which the light energy travels; it is everywhere **normal** to the wavefront.

The distinction is one of dimension and of what each describes: a wavefront is a surface and carries information about phase, while a ray is a line and carries information about direction. A point source emits spherical wavefronts with radially outward rays; far from the source those wavefronts flatten into planes and the rays become parallel.

**(ii) Huygens' principle and the law of reflection.**

*The principle.* Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary disturbance, and the secondary wavelets spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave. The new position of the wavefront after a time \(t\) is the common tangent — the envelope — to all these secondary wavelets.

*Verifying the law of reflection.* Let a plane wavefront AB travel towards a reflecting surface MN, meeting it first at A while B has still to travel the distance BC to reach the surface at C. Let \(v\) be the speed of the wave and \(t\) the time BC takes, so

\(BC = vt\)

While B covers BC, the secondary wavelet from A has expanded into a hemisphere of the same radius:

\(AE = vt\)

The reflected wavefront is the tangent from C to this sphere, namely EC.

Now compare triangles EAC and BAC:

- \(AE = BC = vt\),
- \(\angle AEC = \angle ABC = 90^\circ\) (a wavefront is perpendicular to its ray),
- AC is common.

The two right-angled triangles are therefore **congruent**, so

\(\angle BAC = \angle ECA\)

These are precisely the angle of incidence \(i\) and the angle of reflection \(r\), measured between the wavefronts and the surface — equivalently between the rays and the normal. Hence

\(\angle i = \angle r\)

and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in one plane, which is the plane of the diagram.

**(iii) Wavelength from the fringe positions.**

The \(n^{\text{th}}\) bright fringe sits at \(x_n = \dfrac{n D \lambda}{d}\), and the \(n^{\text{th}}\) dark fringe at \(x_n = \left(n - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{D\lambda}{d}\).

So

\(x_{4\,\text{bright}} = \dfrac{4D\lambda}{d}, \qquad x_{2\,\text{dark}} = \dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{D\lambda}{d}\)

Their separation is given as 5 mm:

\(\dfrac{4D\lambda}{d} - \dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{D\lambda}{d} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(\dfrac{5}{2}\dfrac{D\lambda}{d} = 5 \times 10^{-3}\)

With \(D = 1{\cdot}0\) m and \(d = 3\ \mathrm{mm} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\) m:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3} \times 3 \times 10^{-3} \times 2}{5 \times 1{\cdot}0} = 6 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}\)

**\(\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-6}\) m**, which is \(6\ \mu\)m.

Worth noticing what that number is: \(6\ \mu\)m lies well into the infrared, not the visible range of \(400\)–\(700\) nm. The arithmetic follows the data faithfully, but the data as printed do not describe visible light — with slits 3 mm apart and a screen 1 m away, a visible wavelength would put the two fringes about \(0{\cdot}5\) mm apart rather than 5 mm.

rows.stem:
(i) A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 'K' and thickness 't' is inserted between plates of a parallel plate capacitor of plate separation d and plate area A. Obtain an expression for its capacitance.
(ii) Two capacitors of different capacitances are connected first (1) in series and then (2) in parallel across a dc source of 100 V. If the total energy stored in the combination in the two cases are 40 mJ and 250 mJ respectively, find the capacitance of the capacitors.
rows.solution:
**(i) Capacitance with a partially filling dielectric slab.**

The slab of thickness \(t\) does not fill the gap \(d\), so the field between the plates has two different values along the path from one plate to the other.

In the air gaps, of total thickness \((d - t)\):

\(E_0 = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)

Inside the dielectric, the polarisation reduces the field by the factor \(K\):

\(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0 K}\)

The potential difference is the sum of the drops across the two regions:

\(V = E_0(d - t) + E\,t = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}(d - t) + \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0 K}\,t\)

\(V = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\left[d - t + \dfrac{t}{K}\right] = \dfrac{q}{A\varepsilon_0}\left[d - t + \dfrac{t}{K}\right]\)

Hence

\(C = \dfrac{q}{V} = \dfrac{A\varepsilon_0}{d - t + \dfrac{t}{K}} = \dfrac{A\varepsilon_0}{d - t\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{K}\right)}\)

The formula passes both limits: with \(t = 0\) it gives \(A\varepsilon_0/d\), and with \(t = d\) it gives \(KA\varepsilon_0/d\). Note also that the slab's *position* in the gap never enters — only its thickness — so sliding it about changes nothing.

**(ii) Finding the two capacitances.**

With \(V = 100\) V, so \(V^{2} = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{V^{2}}\):

*Series:* the equivalent capacitance is \(\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\), and

\(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2}\right)(10^{4}) = 40 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2} = 8 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{F} = 8\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)

*Parallel:*

\(\dfrac{1}{2}(C_1 + C_2)(10^{4}) = 250 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(C_1 + C_2 = 5 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{F} = 50\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)

Combining the two results gives the product:

\(C_1C_2 = 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 \times 10^{-5} = 4 \times 10^{-10}\)

So \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are the roots of

\(x^{2} - (5 \times 10^{-5})x + 4 \times 10^{-10} = 0\)

\(x = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-5} \pm \sqrt{25 \times 10^{-10} - 16 \times 10^{-10}}}{2} = \dfrac{(5 \pm 3) \times 10^{-5}}{2}\)

\(C_1 = 4 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{F} = 40\ \mu\mathrm{F}, \qquad C_2 = 1 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{F} = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)

The two energies differ by a factor of \(6{\cdot}25\), and that ratio is what pins the capacitances: parallel always stores more, since the same voltage sits across a larger total capacitance.

rows.stem:
(i) Using Gauss's law, show that the electric field \(\vec{E}\) at a point due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet is given by \(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}\) where symbols have their usual meanings.
(ii) Electric field \(\vec{E}\) in a region is given by
\(\vec{E} = (5x^2 + 2)\hat{i}\)
where E is in N/C and \(x\) is in meters.
A cube of side 10 cm is placed in the region as shown in figure.
Calculate (1) the electric flux through the cube, and (2) the net charge enclosed by the cube.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED for sub-part (ii) — the flux depends on WHERE along the x-axis the cube sits and how its faces are oriented, and the stem says only 'as shown in figure'. What is drawn: a right-handed axis triad with y up, x to the right and z toward the lower-left; a cube drawn in oblique projection with one vertex at the marked origin 0 and its edges parallel to the three axes; and, to the right of the cube, an arrow labelled \(\vec{E}\) with a second arrow labelled \(\hat{i}\) beneath it, both pointing along \(+x\). Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
**(i) Field of a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.**

Let the sheet carry surface charge density \(\sigma\). By symmetry the field must be perpendicular to the sheet, directed away from it on both sides (for positive \(\sigma\)), and its magnitude can depend only on the distance from the sheet.

Choose as the Gaussian surface a cylinder — a "pillbox" — of cross-sectional area \(A\), placed with its axis normal to the sheet and its two flat faces equidistant on either side.

*Flux.* Over the curved side \(\vec{E}\) is parallel to the surface, so \(\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = 0\) there and it contributes nothing. Over each flat face \(\vec{E}\) is parallel to the outward normal and uniform, so each contributes \(EA\):

\(\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \int_1 \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} + \int_2 \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = EA + EA = 2EA\)

*Charge enclosed.* The pillbox cuts out an area \(A\) of the sheet, so \(q = \sigma A\).

*Gauss's law.*

\(2EA = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\)

Vectorially, with \(\hat{n}\) the unit normal pointing away from the sheet:

\(\vec{E} = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\hat{n}\)

The factor of 2 in the denominator is the flux being shared between two faces, and the striking feature is that \(E\) is **independent of distance** — an infinite sheet produces a uniform field, because moving further away gains you a proportionately larger area of contributing charge.

**(ii) Flux through the cube, and the charge inside.**

The field \(\vec{E} = (5x^{2} + 2)\hat{i}\) points along \(x\) everywhere, so only the two faces perpendicular to \(x\) carry any flux — on the other four, \(\vec{E}\) lies in the plane of the face. From the figure the cube has one corner at the origin with edges along the axes, so those two faces sit at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 0{\cdot}10\) m, each of area

\(A = (0{\cdot}10)^{2} = 1 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)

*Left face, \(x = 0\).* Here \(E = 5(0)^{2} + 2 = 2\) N/C, and the outward normal points along \(-\hat{i}\), so the flux is negative:

\(\phi_L = -2 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)

*Right face, \(x = 0{\cdot}10\) m.* Here \(E = 5(0{\cdot}10)^{2} + 2 = 0{\cdot}05 + 2 = 2{\cdot}05\) N/C, with the outward normal along \(+\hat{i}\):

\(\phi_R = +2{\cdot}05 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)

**(1) Net flux:**

\(\phi = \phi_L + \phi_R = (2{\cdot}05 - 2) \times 10^{-2} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)

**(2) Charge enclosed,** from Gauss's law:

\(q = \varepsilon_0\,\phi = 8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-12} \times 5 \times 10^{-4} = 4{\cdot}43 \times 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{C}\)

The whole answer rests on a small difference between two much larger numbers, and that is the physics rather than an accident: a *uniform* field would give exactly equal and opposite contributions and enclose no charge. It is the fact that \(E\) varies with \(x\) — that the field is stronger where it leaves than where it enters — that requires charge inside.

rows.stem:
(i) Mention the factors on which the resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit depends. Plot a graph showing variation of impedance of a series LCR circuit with the frequency of the applied a.c. source.
(ii) With the help of a suitable diagram, explain the working of a step-up transformer.
(iii) Write two causes of energy loss in a real transformer.
rows.solution:
**(i) Resonant frequency and the impedance curve.**

At resonance in a series LCR circuit the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, \(X_L = X_C\), giving

\(\omega_0 L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_0 C} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \nu_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\)

So the resonant frequency depends on the **inductance L** and the **capacitance C** alone. It does **not** depend on the resistance — R governs how sharp the resonance is, never where it sits.

*The graph.* Plotting impedance \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}}\) against frequency gives a U-shaped curve. At low frequency \(X_C\) is huge and \(Z\) is large; as the frequency rises \(Z\) falls, reaching a **minimum of exactly \(R\)** at \(\nu = \nu_0\); beyond resonance \(X_L\) dominates and \(Z\) climbs again. The curve never touches the frequency axis, since \(Z\) cannot fall below \(R\).

**(ii) Working of a step-up transformer.**

*Construction.* Two coils — a primary of \(N_p\) turns and a secondary of \(N_s\) turns — are wound on a common laminated soft-iron core. In a step-up transformer \(N_s > N_p\).

*Working.* An alternating voltage applied across the primary drives an alternating current, which sets up an alternating magnetic flux in the core. The soft iron confines that flux and carries it almost entirely to the secondary, so the same flux \(\phi\) links every turn of both coils. By Faraday's law each turn has the same emf \(-d\phi/dt\) induced in it, so the total emf in each coil is proportional to its number of turns:

\(\varepsilon_p = -N_p\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}, \qquad \varepsilon_s = -N_s\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}\)

Since \(N_s > N_p\), the secondary voltage exceeds the primary voltage — the voltage is stepped up.

Energy is not created. For an ideal transformer \(V_pI_p = V_sI_s\), so the current is stepped **down** in exactly the same ratio. A transformer works only on alternating current: a steady current produces a constant flux, and a constant flux induces nothing.

**(iii) Two causes of energy loss in a real transformer.**

*Eddy currents.* The changing flux induces circulating currents in the iron core itself, which dissipate energy as heat. Laminating the core reduces but does not eliminate them.

*Hysteresis.* Taking the core around its magnetisation loop each cycle costs energy proportional to the loop's area, again lost as heat. Using soft iron, with a narrow loop, keeps this small.

(Copper loss in the winding resistances, and flux leakage where not all the primary's flux reaches the secondary, are the other two standard causes.)

rows.stem:
(i) With the help of a diagram, briefly explain the construction and working of ac generator.
(ii) An electron is revolving around a proton in an orbit of radius r with a speed v. Obtain expression for magnetic moment associated with the electron.
rows.solution:
**(i) The ac generator.**

*Construction.* An ac generator consists of a rectangular coil — the armature, of many turns — mounted on a rotor shaft and free to rotate in a uniform magnetic field supplied by permanent magnets or an electromagnet. The two ends of the coil are connected to two separate **slip rings**, against which carbon brushes press to carry the output to the external circuit.

The slip rings are the defining component: because each end of the coil stays permanently connected to its own ring, the output reverses along with the emf, and the current delivered is alternating. (A split-ring commutator in the same position would reverse the connections every half turn and give direct current instead.)

*Working.* The coil is rotated in the field by some external agency. As it turns, the angle between its plane and the field changes continuously, so the flux linked with it changes, and by Faraday's law an emf is induced.

Taking \(\theta = \omega t\) as the angle between the coil's normal and the field, the flux linkage is

\(\phi = NBA\cos\omega t\)

and the induced emf is

\(\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\,\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t\)

The emf is therefore sinusoidal, reversing twice per revolution. It is greatest when the coil's plane is **parallel** to the field — where the flux is momentarily zero but changing fastest — and zero when the plane is perpendicular to it.

**(ii) Magnetic moment of the revolving electron.**

An electron going round its orbit is a current: the whole charge \(e\) passes any point of the orbit once per revolution. With orbital circumference \(2\pi r\) and speed \(v\), the period is \(T = 2\pi r / v\), so the equivalent current is

\(I = \dfrac{q}{T} = \dfrac{e}{\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}} = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r}\)

A current loop of area \(A\) has magnetic moment \(m = IA\), and here \(A = \pi r^{2}\):

\(m = \dfrac{ev}{2\pi r} \times \pi r^{2}\)

\(m = \dfrac{1}{2}evr\)

The result is worth pairing with the electron's orbital angular momentum \(L = m_e v r\). Dividing one by the other gives

\(\dfrac{m}{L} = \dfrac{e}{2m_e}\)

a ratio fixed by two fundamental constants and independent of the orbit — the gyromagnetic ratio. It is what makes magnetic moment and angular momentum two views of the same thing for an orbiting charge, and combining it with Bohr's quantisation \(L = nh/2\pi\) gives the Bohr magneton.
